lines: Picture a consumer that watches one order go by twice: it sees the cancellation land before the creation.
Nothing about the consumer itself is broken.
Something about where those two records landed changed, and that's the whole mystery this reel untangles.
Think of each lane here as its own private queue, walled off from its neighbors.
A queue keeps its own line perfectly straight.
What it never does on its own is tell another queue anything at all about who went first.
Worth sitting with before the reveal settles it.
These two records never share a lane.
Does sharing a producer, or just living in the same topic, buy them any relationship once they're written?
answer: No relationship at all, however the two records were sent.
Order is strictly a property of one lane by itself.
Sharing a producer, or a topic, or anything else, creates nothing between two different lanes' own orderings.

lines: Notice what actually draws the boundary here: it isn't the topic, and it isn't the producer.
It's the lane itself.
Step outside one lane and the ordering promise simply stops existing, the same way a page number means nothing once you've picked up a different book.
Here's the trickier case: a line can fail and get resent, while a line right behind it sails through untouched on the first try.
Before watching the numbers, ask what a system that owes you nothing but per-lane order is actually allowed to do with that gap.
answer: It's allowed to let the faster line land first, slipping ahead of the one still being retried.
Unless one setting changes that, a resend can be accepted after a batch that never even needed a second try.

lines: Watch the gap close, measured rather than assumed.
Left alone, the resend really does slot in after its faster neighbor, out of turn.
Flip one setting, and the broker itself starts refusing a duplicate acceptance, pinning the resend right back to where it belongs.
That protection isn't unconditional, and the ceiling is worth remembering precisely.
It holds only up to five outstanding requests at once.
That's as many unacknowledged attempts the broker is willing to track per sender before the bookkeeping itself would have to be trusted blindly.
This is the quieter failure mode, and it has nothing to do with retries at all.
Grow the lane count, and the formula deciding which lane a label belongs to shifts for everyone.
One label can keep its old spot by pure coincidence. Most won't, and nothing physically carries their history over for them.
None of those numbers were asserted for effect.
They came out of a script that actually ran the comparison and the hash check moments before this frame even existed.
That's the only reason they're trustworthy enough to build an intuition on.
Step back and the whole shape is one idea with two edges.
A hard guarantee inside a lane, and total silence between lanes.
Plus a mapping from label to lane that the lane count itself can quietly redraw whenever it changes.
